editorialSections.title: In regulated categories, the words carry the risk

blocks.text: A supplement that says it "supports focus" sits in one world. The same product that says it "treats ADHD" sits in another, where the FDA reads it as an unapproved drug claim and the FTC asks for the substantiation behind it. The line between the two is language, and it moves fast. This checker gives your copy a first pass, surfacing the phrases that tend to attract a second look so a person can decide what to do about them.
What it checks

Disease and medical claims, structure-function overreach, substantiation gaps, deceptive consumer-protection patterns, and the superlatives and absolutes that draw scrutiny. Each match is tied to a category, a risk level, and the regulator whose zone it touches.
What it can't do

It cannot tell you whether copy is lawful, and it gives no legal advice. It matches language to curated patterns and explains why each pattern tends to draw attention. It misses claims phrased in ways the lexicon does not cover, and it flags some phrases that context makes fine. A qualified human decides.

editorialSections.title: Five categories, mapped to the regulators who care

blocks.text: Each flag names the category the phrase falls into, a risk level, and the regulator whose attention zone it tends to touch. The overall risk score weights High findings heaviest, then Medium, then Low.
Disease / medical claims
Language that says a product treats, cures, prevents, or diagnoses a named condition. This is the fast path to being read as an unapproved drug.
Structure-function overreach
Therapeutic framing beyond a permitted structure-function statement: "heals," "clinically proven," "doctor recommended," and similar.
Substantiation gaps
Proof claims with no qualifier behind them: "studies show," "proven," "guaranteed," "100%," "#1." The FTC asks what backs them.
Deceptive patterns
Consumer-protection triggers: "miracle," "risk-free," "no side effects," and "FDA approved" used where it does not apply.
Superlatives & absolutes
Unqualified absolutes like "always," "never fails," "completely safe," and "the best." They raise the bar on what you must be able to prove.

editorialSections.title: The confusion is usually about structure, not facts

blocks.text: Most people who ask "is this legal?" are actually missing the map: two governments regulate in parallel, several agencies each own a different piece, and status can move through a rulemaking process that most explainers skip. This tool teaches the map. Once you understand how a substance is classified and who controls that classification, you know exactly where to look for the current answer, and you know why a headline about one state does not settle the question.
What it explains

The five-schedule system and the criteria behind each schedule, the split roles of the DEA and FDA, the FDA-to-DEA scheduling recommendation process, the federal-state divergence pattern, and how a substance is moved between schedules through petition, review, and rulemaking.
What it will not do

It will not assert any substance's current legal status in any jurisdiction as authoritative, and it will not give legal advice. Status changes, and a stale claim relied on is a real risk. Every explanation ends by routing you to primary sources and to a licensed attorney for the current, specific answer.

editorialSections.title: Four things everyone gets wrong, made clear

blocks.text: Each explanation is built from these stable structural pieces. None of them depend on a specific state's current status, which is exactly why they stay useful while the headlines change.
Five tiers, defined by criteria
Schedules I through V rank substances by accepted medical use and potential for abuse. The schedule sets the federal controls; it is not the same thing as "banned" or "allowed."
DEA, FDA, and the states
The DEA schedules and enforces, the FDA approves drugs and makes scheduling recommendations, and each state runs its own parallel program. Different agencies, different questions.
How status actually moves
A substance changes schedule through petition, FDA scientific review, a DEA recommendation request, proposed rulemaking, a public comment period, and a final rule. It is a process, not a switch.
Why federal and state disagree
Federal and state law operate in parallel. A substance can be federally controlled while states run their own separate programs, which is why one headline never settles the question.
Where the current answer lives
Every explanation ends by pointing you to the Federal Register, the DEA, the FDA, the relevant state agencies, and a licensed attorney for the point-in-time, jurisdiction-specific answer.
No claims that go stale
The tool avoids stating any state's current specific status as authoritative. It teaches the pattern so you can read the current sources yourself, correctly.

editorialSections.title: The claim type tells you what evidence it owes you

blocks.text: "People say it helped their nausea" and "it cures nausea" are different kinds of statements, and they carry very different burdens. One reports experience. The other asserts cause and effect, which is the kind of claim that a controlled trial exists to test. When you can name the claim type, you can ask the right question of the evidence behind it. This tool does that first pass for you, so a person can decide what to make of a claim before repeating it.
What it does

Reads the language of a claim for signal words, classifies it (causal, mechanism, correlation, anecdotal, or overstated), and maps that type to the tier of evidence it would take to support it. It explains the evidence hierarchy, lists common confounders to check, and hands you questions to ask before repeating the claim.
What it does not do

It does not judge whether a claim is true or false. It gives no medical advice, no diagnosis, no treatment or dosing guidance, and no health recommendation. It cannot read a study for you or grade the actual evidence that exists. It classifies the language and points you toward the primary literature and qualified people who can.

editorialSections.title: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome, read as an evidence question

blocks.text: CHS comes up often in cannabis reporting, and it is a useful case for practicing evidence literacy. The panel below describes only what the published evidence base discusses and how strong that evidence is generally understood to be. It is a description of the literature, not a claim about your health.
What the evidence base discusses

The published literature describes Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS) as a pattern of recurrent, cyclic nausea and vomiting reported in some people with long-term, frequent cannabis use. Reports in the literature also describe symptoms easing after people stop using cannabis. Some case reports note that hot showers or baths are associated with temporary symptom relief. These are the recurring features the evidence base talks about at a high level.

Much of the CHS literature is built from case reports and case series, which sit on the lower rungs of the evidence hierarchy. That body of work is useful for describing a pattern and generating hypotheses. It is weaker for establishing cause and effect than controlled studies would be. Reviews of CHS commonly note that diagnostic criteria and mechanisms are still debated and that higher-tier evidence is limited. Reading any single CHS claim well means asking which tier of evidence stands behind it.

items: Is the source a case report, a case series, an observational study, or a systematic review, and how far does that tier let the claim reach?
Does the claim describe an association that was reported, or does it assert that cannabis use caused the symptoms?
Were other causes of cyclic vomiting considered and ruled out in the source?
Is a reported improvement after stopping cannabis presented as observed, or as proven cause and effect?
How large and how representative was the group the claim is based on?
Primary literature: search PubMed and Google Scholar for "cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome" and read the studies and reviews themselves rather than summaries of them.
Qualified people: a physician, gastroenterologist, or toxicologist can speak to an individual situation. This tool cannot.

blocks.text: This description is educational and general. It is not a statement about any individual and it is not medical advice.

editorialSections.title: Five claim types, mapped to the evidence they owe

blocks.text: The analyzer looks for the signal words that mark each claim type, then explains what tier of evidence a claim of that type would need and what confounders to check. It never grades the underlying science. It grades the language and points you at the questions.
Causal claims
"Causes," "cures," "prevents," "treats." Asserts cause and effect. Needs controlled trials, ideally more than one, not case reports or testimonials.
Mechanism claims
"Works by," "binds to," "activates receptors." A plausible mechanism is not proof of a clinical effect. Ask whether the effect itself was measured in people.
Correlation / association
"Linked to," "associated with," "users report lower." Association is not causation. Check for confounders, reverse causation, and selection effects.
Anecdotal framing
"People report," "I felt," "many say." Experience is real data, but a single tier of it cannot carry a causal or population claim.
Absolute / overstated language
"Proven," "guaranteed," "100%," "miracle." Absolutes raise the bar of proof and rarely survive contact with the actual evidence.
The evidence hierarchy
Case report, then case series, then observational study, then randomized controlled trial, then systematic review and meta-analysis. Higher rungs control more bias.

editorialSections.title: People chase a better prompt when they need a repeatable workflow

blocks.text: A prompt tells a model what to do once. A workflow says what goes in, where the facts come from, who checks the output, and where the result gets stored. When the same prompt gives uneven results, wording is rarely the problem. The missing parts are inputs, grounding, a verification step, a human-review checkpoint, and a home for the output. This converter turns a prompt into that scaffold so the work runs the same way every time.
What it produces

Seven sections filled with task-aware defaults: inputs required, source and grounding requirements, a step sequence, a QA step with a named human-review checkpoint, output format and storage, reuse notes for templatizing, and risk flags.
What it can't do

It cannot run the workflow, judge your output, or replace review by a qualified person. It reads keywords and drafts a scaffold you edit. Treat it as a starting structure, not a finished operating procedure.

editorialSections.title: Seven sections, every time

blocks.text: A prompt gives you words. A workflow gives you a repeatable structure. The converter fills each of these seven sections with defaults tuned to the task it detects, so nothing important gets skipped.
Inputs required
The facts and materials the task needs before it starts, so the same run does not depend on memory.
Source / grounding
Where the content must come from, so the output rests on real sources rather than invention.
Step sequence
The ordered steps that turn inputs into a draft, written so anyone can follow them.
Verification / QA
The checks the output must pass, including a named human-review checkpoint before it is used.
Output & storage
The format of the result and where it gets stored, so the work is findable and reusable.
Reuse notes
How to templatize the run: which parts change each time and which stay fixed.
Risk flags
The traps to watch: confidential data in unapproved tools, and output that needs source verification before use.

editorialSections.title: 1. Orchestration — Harvey is one node, not the system

blocks.text: Firms are not buying a single model. They are wiring several drafting and research tools into their workflow. Without a governing layer, each one can put an unverified authority in front of a court. The Trust-Safe Operating Layer sits between those tools and the filing/review system.

Example stack shown for illustration. The two AI research assistants are CoCounsel Legal (grounded in Westlaw / Thomson Reuters) and Lexis+ with Protégé (grounded in LexisNexis); Harvey's own research alliance is with LexisNexis. The layer is tool-agnostic and maps to whatever the firm actually runs.
Harvey is one node, not the system. The governance and evaluation layer is the product.

Methodology note (illustrative)

Jurisdiction accuracy: share of tasks that apply the controlling jurisdiction's rule correctly.
Citation pass rate: share of cited authorities that clear structural and existence checks.

editorialSections.title: 5. Adoption — where 2026 pilots actually fail

blocks.text: The technology rarely fails; adoption does. Trust is a neurological state: repeated safe exposure lowers threat response and builds the habit loop. Set an estimated adoption rate per stage to see where your funnel leaks.
Three change-management levers

items: Safe exposure: low-stakes, reversible first tasks so the threat response never fires. Trust is built by repetition, not by a training deck.
Visible governance: when lawyers can see the verification gate and audit trail, the tool feels like a safeguard rather than a liability — converting exposure into trust.
Peer advocacy: a respected internal champion who demonstrates wins moves habitual users to advocates faster than any top-down mandate.

blocks.text: Where 2026 pilots actually fail: the drop-off between trust and habitual use, not the model quality.
